summary: Describes use cases for Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI) that correspond to industry needs and that open interfaces and protocols would support. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This lists reasons why different delivery companies would want to cooperate, such as covering more places or handling busy times together.

subtitle: Why separate content delivery networks would want to work together, and what that would be used for.

tldr.problem: Each Content Delivery Network is a stand-alone network, so a provider cannot easily borrow another's reach, capacity or capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists use cases for CDN Interconnection (CDNI) in three groups, footprint extension, offload and capability, plus the content delivery policies that must be enforced across all of them.
tldr.outcome: It is meant to motivate CDNI requirements, and it obsoletes RFC 3570, which used slightly different terminology and models.

today: RFC 6770 is an Informational RFC and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It obsoleted RFC 3570 to avoid confusion over terminology and models.

sections.title: Why Interconnect CDNs
sections.content:
A Content Delivery Network (CDN) improves the End User's experience (lower latency, more robustness), reduces network operators' costs for cacheable content, and reduces Content Service Provider (CSP) infrastructure costs. Today, however, each CDN is a stand-alone network. The aim of CDN Interconnection is that interconnected CDNs collectively behave as a single delivery infrastructure.

In the RFC's example, CSP-1 has an agreement with CDN Provider A, and A and B agree to interconnect. When a user requests CSP-1 content, CDN-A can redirect the request to CDN-B, for instance because CDN-B is an Access CDN (one with Surrogates in the same administrative network as the user), and CDN-B delivers it. The user gets better quality of experience, A needs a less extensive CDN, B may be compensated, and CSP-1 needs only one business and technical arrangement. A second CSP, CSP-2, might not want B to carry its content at all, so policy matters.
sections.eli5: If your delivery company does not go to a far-away town, it asks a friend company there to drop off the parcel. You only deal with one company, but the parcel still arrives quickly.

sections.title: Footprint Extension Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC calls footprint extension a major use case. There are four variants:

  • Geographic extension: reach more regions without compromising quality, paying extra transit, or building Surrogates where volume does not justify it. Its example is a French CSP whose French CDN Provider partners with one covering North Africa.
  • Inter-affiliates: a large provider's subsidiaries run separate CDNs, possibly on different technologies, that must interoperate.
  • ISP handling of third-party content: an ISP acting as an Access CDN caches and delivers content injected by an Authoritative CDN, which can cut load, hardware and cost for several parties.
  • Nomadic users: a user away from her home ISP, such as on WiFi or a mobile network, can still get her home content from the CDN in the other network, subject to the CSP's policies such as geo-blocking.
sections.eli5: Four ways friends help each other reach more places: covering far-off countries, sister companies working together, a local post office handling the parcels, and following you when you travel.

sections.title: Offload and Resiliency
sections.content:
In overload handling, a CDN dimensioned for an expected peak can hit a flash crowd and interconnect to use another CDN's capacity. CDNs with different peak times can use each other's resources, which brings dimensioning savings. Planned cases include maintenance or a special event; the Delivering CDN must be able to handle the offloaded requests, so the upstream CDN may need information about downstream CDN capacity.

For failure of delivery resources, a CDN has three options: use internal mechanisms, forward requests to the CSP's origin servers, or redirect to another CDN. The last is a CDNI use case. For content acquisition resiliency, a CDN may fetch from the CSP origin or from a Surrogate in an upstream CDN, and may switch or balance between sources when one fails. Content acquisition protocols themselves are beyond the scope of CDNI.
sections.eli5: When too many people want the same thing at once, or a warehouse breaks down, a friend company can step in and deliver for you.

sections.title: Capability Use Cases
sections.content:
A CDN with the right footprint may still lack a capability and use interconnection to borrow it. The RFC's examples include a CDN that cannot support a delivery protocol such as HTTPS, one with fixed-line coverage that wants to reach mobile devices, and one that supports only IPv4 internally but wants to deliver over native IPv6 through a partner.

Interconnection also helps with technology and vendor interoperability: migrating to a new CDN technology, running a multi-vendor strategy, or deploying a separate CDN for a particular CSP or network. And for QoE and QoS, some CSPs pay a premium for enhanced delivery, so a provider may partner with an Access CDN that can meet the CSP's service-level requirements.
sections.eli5: If your company cannot do something, such as carry a certain kind of package, a friend company that can do it carries it for you.

sections.title: Delivery Policy and Security
sections.content:
An aspect common to every use case is that CSPs want to enforce content delivery policies about when, how and to whom content is delivered. These apply to all interconnected CDNs. Appendix A gives examples: time windows, user agent platform, resolution, authorization, access network and geo-blocking constraints. The delivery network need not understand the business reasons; policies can be distilled into simple rules, such as checking an authorization token, that every downstream CDN enforces.

The appendix also covers secure access (a CSP may require HTTPS or URL signing) and branding (a CSP may want URIs under its own domain name even when other CDNs deliver). The Security Considerations section says the document does not analyze threats, which are discussed in RFC 6707.
sections.eli5: The sender can set rules, like "only deliver on weekdays" or "only in this country," and every friend company that helps must follow them.

viz.caption: THE THREE FAMILIES OF CDNI USE CASES (RFC 6770)

items.title: Footprint extension
items.text: Reach more regions or users: geographic extension, inter-affiliates, ISP handling of third-party content, nomadic users.

items.title: Offload
items.text: Overload handling and dimensioning, failure of delivery resources, content acquisition resiliency.

items.title: Capability
items.text: Device and network technology extension, technology and vendor interoperability, QoE and QoS improvement.
